parts.spoken_English: In June 1984 Alexey Pajitnov, a 29-year-old Moscow coder, grew engrossed in a diversion he had built.
His primitive Elektronika 60 had a purely textual display, so every geometric piece of four tiles was assembled from characters.
He called it Tetris, a fusion of the Greek tetra- and tennis, his favourite pastime.
In the Soviet Union, the state, not its salaried designer, was the proprietor of this intellectual property, and Pajitnov held no entitlement to it.
Copies mushroomed freely on floppy disks across the Eastern bloc.
In 1986 Robert Stein, an enterprising British software vendor, stumbled upon Tetris in Hungary.
In his ignorance of Elorg, the state bureau regulating Soviet software exports, he hastily hawked rights he did not yet legitimately hold.
The rights were shuffled onward through a chaotic muddle of overlapping deals among Western firms, one owned by the magnate Robert Maxwell.
In February 1989 Henk Rogers, a resourceful Dutch-born publisher, reached Moscow on a tourist visa and found his way to Elorg.
Stein and Kevin Maxwell, the magnate's son, were in Moscow that same hectic week of negotiations, each a bidder.
Pajitnov felt a fondness for Rogers, and Nintendo scooped the handheld rights, then worldwide console rights.
Nintendo bundled Tetris with its pocket-sized Game Boy, and that version shipped over 35 million copies.
Pajitnov reaped none of the spoils for years.
His earnings began only after his arrangement's expiry around 1995.
In 1996 he and Rogers founded The Tetris Company to manage the rights.
The man whose puzzle once spread for nothing later helped decide who could sell it.
